name: Israel
summary: Founded in 1948 as a Jewish state in part of British-mandate Palestine; its founding displaced about 700,000 Palestinians (the Nakba); wars with Arab neighbours and the Israeli–Palestinian conflict continue.

knownFor.label: Western Wall
knownFor.note: Holy site of Judaism in Jerusalem.

location.value: At the eastern end of the Mediterranean Sea; about 20,770 km² within the 1949 armistice lines.

terrain.value: From the Negev desert in the south to the fertile Jezreel Valley and the mountains of Galilee and Carmel in the north; most people live on the coastal plain.

climate.value: Mediterranean on the coast, with cool, rainy winters and long, hot summers; semi-arid to desert in the south.

resources.value: Natural gas from offshore fields, produced since 2004.

disasters.value: Destructive earthquakes strike about every 80 years.

urbanisation.value: Four major metropolitan areas: Tel Aviv (Gush Dan), Jerusalem, Haifa and Beersheba.

disease.value: Advanced health care; universal health care since the 1995 National Healthcare Law.

migration.value: Waves of Jewish immigration from 1881; later Holocaust survivors, Jews from Arab and Muslim countries, and immigrants from Ethiopia and the former Soviet Union.

economicBase.value: High technology; leading exports include machinery, software, cut diamonds and farm products.

tradeRoutes.value: Three main ports: Haifa, Ashdod and Eilat (on the Red Sea).

wealth.value: A rich country: the third richest in Asia by income per person.

inequality.value: Large gaps between the capital and rural areas.

governmentType.value: A parliamentary system with a 120-member parliament, the Knesset.

keyRulers.value: David Ben-Gurion. Golda Meir. Yitzhak Rabin. Benjamin Netanyahu.

succession.value: Elections by proportional representation; the prime minister is usually the leader of the largest party.

eliteConflict.value: Competition between political parties and leaders.

majorWars.value: Wars of 1948, 1956, 1967, 1973; Lebanon; Gaza wars, including from 2023.

territoryChange.value: In the 1967 Six-Day War Israel captured and occupied the West Bank, Gaza Strip, Sinai and Golan Heights; the Sinai was returned to Egypt in 1982.

alliancesRivals.value: Close to the US; peace with Egypt (1979) and Jordan (1994).

inventions.value: No major inventions are associated with the modern state.

scienceEducation.value: Strong universities such as the Technion, Hebrew University and Weizmann Institute; Israel spends a larger share of its economy on research than any other country.

openness.value: Open to trade and foreign investment, with periods of restriction.

communicationTransport.value: Three international airports, led by Ben Gurion Airport; ports at Haifa, Ashdod and Eilat.

religion.value: About 73.5% Jewish, 18.1% Muslim, 1.9% Christian and 1.6% Druze (2022).

languageWriting.value: Hebrew, the only revived official language in the world; Arabic has a “special status”.

artsArchitecture.value: Bauhaus buildings by German Jewish architects; the White City of Tel Aviv is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

socialStructure.value: Jewish and Arab citizens; Jewish Israelis range from secular (about half) to traditional, religious and ultra-Orthodox.

sharedIdentity.value: Contested between Jewish, Israeli and Palestinian identities.

dailyLife.value: Foods such as falafel, hummus, shakshouka and couscous.

neighbours.value: Lebanon, Syria, Jordan and Egypt; the West Bank and the Gaza Strip.

ideasReligions.value: Zionism, a movement to re-establish a Jewish homeland in Palestine.

colonisation.value: Ottoman rule from 1516; the British Mandate of Palestine (1920–48).

declineSignals.value: None that define the country as a whole.

overallCertainty.value: Basic facts are well documented; many events are described differently by Israeli and Palestinian sources.
